entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms that lasts a few seconds and then vanishes, leaving a trace or none. Its cause is still unexplained.
entries.background: Reports go back centuries, but there are almost no instrument recordings. Dozens of theories exist and none is accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist who wrote Sur le tonnerre in 1837. He was among the first scientists to collect and discuss ball lightning reports.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: German school official who wrote Der Kugelblitz (1923), the only German-language monograph on ball lightning. It gathered many historical reports.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who keeps a database of ball lightning cases and contributed six of the reports compiled here.

entries.name: Stanley Singer
entries.background: Author of the 1971 book The Nature of Ball Lightning, an early major review of the subject.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's network of sensors that records the time, place and strength of lightning strokes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: Germany's lightning detection network, which locates strokes and measures their current.

entries.name: positive lightning stroke
entries.background: A lightning stroke that carries positive charge to the ground. It is rarer than negative lightning and often stronger.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.background: Lightning that travels between a cloud and the earth. Cloud–cloud strokes stay in the sky.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist, member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna. He described a ball lightning he saw in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen. As a child in 1951 he saw spheres fall and melt patches in asphalt, and he later calculated their energy.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale who became president of the US National Academy of Sciences. He is known for his dinosaur fossil discoveries.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German physicist who, with Otto Stern, performed the 1922 experiment showing that atomic magnetism comes in discrete steps. He later taught at Tübingen.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer and later physics professor at the University of Kent. His 1969 Nature report of a glowing sphere drifting down an airliner aisle drew wide attention.

entries.name: Pikes Peak
entries.background: A 4302 m summit in Colorado's Rocky Mountains. Harvard ran a weather station there from 1874 to 1888.

entries.name: Puy de Dôme
entries.background: A 1465 m old volcano in central France with a weather observatory on its summit.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He was killed by lightning in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity, soon after Benjamin Franklin's kite experiment era began.

entries.name: Frankenstein
entries.background: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel about a scientist whose experiments bring a creature to life. It shaped the popular image of the dangerous, daring scientist.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician who founded modern neurology and taught at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. Sigmund Freud studied under him and translated his lectures.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.background: Temporary paralysis, numbness or loss of feeling in the limbs after being struck by or near lightning. It usually passes within hours.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.background: A 1936 report from Dorstone, England, of a red-hot ball that struck a house and fell into a tub of water, which then boiled for minutes. Researchers used it to estimate how much energy a ball lightning holds.

entries.name: Poughquag glass
entries.background: A 2008 New York sighting of a blue sphere near a glass door. Later tests of the glass's glow under light gave a figure for the ball's radiation output.

entries.name: Camp Blanding experiment
entries.background: Experiment at a Florida military base where a rocket pulled a wire to trigger real lightning onto over 100 ground materials. It produced luminous effects but the researchers did not call them ball lightning.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A 2012 recording on the Qinghai Plateau in China. Cameras with a grating that splits light into colours captured a ball lightning and its light lines, showing iron, silicon, calcium, nitrogen and oxygen.

entries.name: Mitino incident
entries.background: A 2015 Moscow event in which three people filmed a glowing object with phones. Comparing the videos fixed its height and path.
